source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models
finding: Founding LLM test of program tracing. A model that must write the machine state after every step (a scratchpad) executes code far better than one that guesses the output directly.
numbers: Synthetic Python programs: direct prediction 11% few-shot and 20% fine-tuned; scratchpad 26.5% few-shot (relaxed scoring criterion) and 41.5% fine-tuned. Polynomial evaluation: direct 8.8% few-shot and 31.8% fine-tuned; scratchpad 20.1% and 50.7%.
limits: 2021 models. Few-shot scratchpad scoring was relaxed (last value of v0 instead of full trace). Absolute execution accuracy stayed low.
agent_relevance: This is the schema's S2 in machine form: write the state after each step on a concrete input. Make the trace a required output slot.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models
finding: Training on real execution traces of real programs gives partial tracing skill; mixing datasets helped most.
numbers: On MBPP-aug the fine-tuned scratchpad model executed 23.4% of tasks correctly; adding single-line or CodeNet data gave gains; best mix (CodeNet + single-line) produced the correct final output for 26.6% of tasks, 24.6% were traced perfectly on all three examples, and about 42% of individual traces were exactly right under greedy decoding.
limits: Only three inputs per task; accuracy under 30% means an unaided model's trace is often wrong.
agent_relevance: A model-written trace is not proof; code should run the program and compare (G2, G3).

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
finding: 800 short Python functions; predict output from input (O) and input from output (I). GPT-4 was best at 67% I and 63% O without chain of thought; best open model 47% I and 44% O.
numbers: N=800 functions, pass@1 at T=0.2. GPT-4 67% (I), 63% (O). Best open-source 47% / 44%. Code Llama 34B with CoT: 50% / 46% (abstract).
limits: Python only, short functions; later saturated (see c27).
agent_relevance: Even simple traces fail often. Do not trust a single unaided mental run.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
finding: Chain of thought helps output prediction (a pure trace task) more than input prediction. GPT-4 gains most; weak models gain little or lose.
numbers: GPT-4 with CoT: 74.8% input, 81.9% output pass@1. CoT helped Code Llama 34B and GPT-4 on both tasks, GPT-3.5 only on output, Code Llama 13B on neither. For Code Llama and GPT-3.5 many items solved directly were lost under CoT; for GPT-4 few were. CoT widened the pass@5 minus pass@1 gap.
limits: Gain depends on model strength.
agent_relevance: Step-by-step execution is worth its tokens only for a strong base model; for weaker ones use code-run to ground the trace.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
finding: Code-writing skill and tracing skill come apart: models distilled from GPT-4 outputs scored high on HumanEval but no better than Code Llama on CRUXEval.
numbers: For base models HumanEval correlates with CRUXEval. For WizardCoder, Phind and Phi (GPT-4-distilled) the trend breaks.
limits: Correlational, two benchmarks.
agent_relevance: A model that writes fluent code may hold a poor machine model. Test answers by running, not by fluency.

source: La Malfa et al. (2024) Code Simulation Challenges for Large Language Models
finding: Models simulate short straight-line code but accuracy falls with length. Logical and/or is much harder than add/sub/mov. Most errors occur when the model outputs only the final value instead of the full trace.
numbers: Programs of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 lines, 3 runs of 30 experiments per setting. GPT-4, LLaMA3-70B and GPT-3.5 reliable on mixed instructions; Jurassic2-Ultra, LLaMA2-70B, CodeLlama-34B fail even on short snippets. Footnote: GPT-4 skipped the trace in more than 95% of cases.
limits: Synthetic assembly-like code, not natural programs.
agent_relevance: Force the full trace in the output slot; reject a bare final answer.

source: La Malfa et al. (2024) Code Simulation Challenges for Large Language Models
finding: Simulation leans on pattern recognition and memorisation. Nested-loop accuracy falls with computational complexity; GPT-4 beyond O(n^2) seems to unroll loops and pattern-match the final value. Sorting simulation also degrades with input length.
numbers: Nested loops up to cubic; 8 sorting routines, input length 10, 20, 30, 40 random integers 0-100.
limits: Unrolling inferred from logs, not verified by probing internals.
agent_relevance: Loops are the weak spot of the model's machine. Use code-run for any loop with many iterations.

source: La Malfa et al. (2024) Code Simulation Challenges for Large Language Models
finding: Chain of Simulation (CoSm) prompt: simulate line by line like a compiler. It helped GPT-4 on straight-line and critical-path code, hurt GPT-4 on nested loops, and did the reverse for LLaMA3-70B. On the synthetic good-exchange task GPT-4 + CoSm reached oracle-like accuracy at medium length.
numbers: Deltas are shown in Figs 13-15; no exact per-setting numbers in the text.
limits: Prompt effect is model-specific and changes sign.
agent_relevance: Test any trace prompt per model at equal tokens (G7); do not assume it helps.

source: Liu and Jabbarvand (2024, v of 2026) CodeMind: Evaluating LLMs for Code Reasoning
finding: Three tasks: execution reasoning (IER), specification reasoning, dynamic semantics reasoning. 13 LLMs on 4 benchmarks. Performance drops with complexity, nested constructs, non-primitive types and intra-class dependencies.
numbers: Reasoning models beat GPT-4 on IER by 14.76 points (Claude-Sonnet-4.6), 11.35 (o4-mini), 9.26 (DeepSeek-R1). Adding one ground-truth input/output to the prompt raised code-synthesis pass@1 by 5.36% on average (9.78% ClassEval, 0.94% HumanEval).
limits: Table cells garbled in my text extraction, so only narrative numbers are reported.
agent_relevance: A concrete test case in the prompt helps writing; supports tracing the spec on an example (S2).

source: Liu and Jabbarvand (2024, v of 2026) CodeMind: Evaluating LLMs for Code Reasoning
finding: Bug-repair success is not correlated with code-reasoning success; many repairs succeed through shortcuts, not through a machine model.
numbers: In manual inspection of successful repairs, 45.00% and 39.58% (two groups: failed all three reasoning tasks, failed one or two) were due to natural-language shortcuts and lucky hallucinations.
limits: Sampled at 95% confidence per model; manual labels.
agent_relevance: A correct fix does not show the model understood execution. Check against real run output (G2).

source: REval authors (2024) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We?
finding: Four step-level tasks (coverage, program state, execution path, output) show models are weak on intermediate machine state and inconsistent across the four.
numbers: Average accuracy over all models 44.4%; average Incremental Consistency score 10.3; IC below 20 for all open-source models. GPT-4-Turbo best with IC 42.5, more than double second place.
limits: Mostly 2024 code LLMs.
agent_relevance: Models answer a step question and the final output inconsistently; code should cross-check the trace against the output.

source: REval authors (2024) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We?
finding: CoT prompting helped execution-path prediction for CodeLlama-7B-Instruct but hurt output prediction.
numbers: EPP accuracy 10.8% to 21.4% with CoT (above the 13B model at 14.4%). Output prediction fell by 6.8 points absolute.
limits: One small model; authors blame a wrong thought chain.
agent_relevance: One bad early step in a trace poisons the end; verify steps, not just the final answer.

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: Teaching Large Language Models to Reason about Code Execution
finding: Putting the real execution trace (variable states per line) in the prompt and training on trace-based rationales raised program-repair fix rate.
numbers: PaLM 2-L: +26.1 points on Mbpp-R (to 49.3%) and +14.3 on HumanEvalFix-Plus. Without traces at test time: 40.8% on Mbpp-R, +21.8 over 3-shot baseline, 3.3 below the with-trace version.
limits: Needs self-training fine-tuning; PaLM 2 only.
agent_relevance: Real-output traces plus short reasoning is the pattern; supports S2 with code-run supplying the trace.

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: Teaching Large Language Models to Reason about Code Execution
finding: Without training, chain of thought over traces did not help and could hurt: models hallucinate details not in the trace.
numbers: CoT vs vanilla with trace: average -7.8% on HumanEvalFix-Plus (DeepSeek Coder 57.3 to 30.5; StarCoder 29.3 to 16.5). Removing traces under CoT: -4.8% (Mbpp-R), -4.3% (HumanEvalFix-Plus). Only about 30% of sampled PaLM 2-L rationales explained the error correctly.
limits: Prompted 2024 models; GPT-4 did not drop in the same way.
agent_relevance: Free reasoning on top of a real trace can be worse than the bare trace. Keep the reasoning slot short.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Code Execution with Pre-trained Language Models (CodeExecutor)
finding: Pre-training on execution traces with curriculum learning lets a model predict real program output and traces far above Codex.
numbers: Tutorial set: output accuracy 76.42% vs Codex 13.07%. Real-world set: 48.06% output, 33.38% exact trace match, +30.6 points output over Codex. Without curriculum: 45.93% output, 30.98% trace. Control flow: 57 of 60 conditionals correct; loops and data structures weaker.
limits: Trained in, 2023.
agent_relevance: Execution state can be learned; loops and data structures remain weaker.

source: Markosyan et al. (2025) What I Cannot Execute, I Do Not Understand: Training and Evaluating LLMs on Program Execution Traces
finding: Execution Tuning on line-level and instruction-level traces. A dynamic scratchpad (state is rewritten each step) beats a scratchpad that accumulates history.
numbers: About 80% on CruxEval and MBPP output prediction. Llama3.1 8B prompted: Line-1 53.8% control flow, 10.6% full state; Line-n global 16.8% control flow. Fine-tuned Line-1: 99.5% / 96.3% full state; Line-n 95.1% / 79.0%. Scratchpad fine-tuned 91.9% with 86.4% full state. Instruction-level prompted stack accuracy 5.8%. Traces up to 14k steps.
limits: Meta models; Python and bytecode traces.
agent_relevance: For long traces, rewrite a compact state each step instead of appending history.

source: Meta FAIR CodeGen Team (2025) CWM: An Open-Weights LLM for Research on Code Generation with World Models
finding: A 32B model mid-trained on Python execution traces (over 120M traced functions) as observation-action pairs, as a world model of code.
numbers: 94.3% CruxEval-Output, 65.8% SWE-bench Verified (with test-time scaling), 68.6% LiveCodeBench-v5, 96.6% Math-500, 76.0% AIME 2024.
limits: I read the abstract, intro and trace-format sections only; the effect of trace data alone is not isolated in what I read.
agent_relevance: Labs are building a notional machine into the model itself, not the prompt.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Rubber-duck debugging loop: the model explains its code and uses run results. Gains of 2-3% on Spider (no unit tests), up to 12% on TransCoder and MBPP, and 9% on the hardest Spider tier.
numbers: MBPP with no execution (Table 3, Codex): baseline 61.4, plain 'simple' feedback 57.6 (worse), +explanation 64.4, +model-written trace 66.2.
limits: Model-written traces carry no run output, so the gain is small. Gains with unit tests are larger.
agent_relevance: Plain 'check again' feedback lowered accuracy: supports G1 and G2, no revision without real output.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) Debug like a Human: A Large Language Model Debugger via Verifying Runtime Execution Step by Step (LDB)
finding: Split the program into basic blocks, give the LLM real intermediate variable values at breakpoints, and have it verify each block.
numbers: Up to +9.8% pass@1 across HumanEval, TransCoder, MBPP with GPT-3.5, CodeLlama and StarCoder. Self-Debugging with model-written explanation or dry-run trace failed to improve seed programs on HumanEval with StarCoder.
limits: Authors say inaccurate model-written traces can misguide debugging.
agent_relevance: Real traces beat model-imagined traces. This is S2 with code-run inside an agent loop.

source: Ding et al. (2024) SemCoder: Training Code Language Models with Comprehensive Semantics Reasoning
finding: Natural-language monologue about execution beat raw state traces as training data; a 6.7B model matched GPT-3.5 on tracing tasks.
numbers: CRUXEval-I 63.6 (GPT-3.5 50.3), CRUXEval-O 63.9 (GPT-3.5 59.0), HumanEval 79.3. Ablation on deepseek-coder-6.7b, CRUX-I / CRUX-O / LCB-Exec: few-shot 39.5/41.2/36.1; scratchpad 48.8/50.6/39.9; NExT-style 49.4/50.9/32.2; concise trace 52.1/55.6/35.9; monologue 61.8/63.5/58.5.
limits: Fine-tuning, one base model.
agent_relevance: Short causal prose per state change may suit a language model better than a raw state dump. Test it in the scaffold.

source: Singla (2023) Evaluating ChatGPT and GPT-4 for Visual Programming
finding: Execution trace on Hour-of-Code maze tasks (a small notional machine with an avatar): GPT-4 produced correct traces on 60% of tasks, ChatGPT on 10%.
numbers: TraceCorrect: ChatGPT 10.0, GPT-4 60.0. TracePartialCorrect 30.0 vs 70.0. TransitionsCorrect 10.0 vs 90.0. SensingCorrect 10.0 vs 60.0. Example: GPT-4 trace looked finished but the avatar crashes into walls.
limits: Small task set, expert annotation, 2023 models, spatial domain.
agent_relevance: A confident trace can be physically impossible; check it against the machine rules in code.

source: Lehtinen, Koutcheme, Hellas (2024) Let's Ask AI About Their Programs: ChatGPT's Answers to Program Comprehension Questions
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 answered multiple-choice questions about code they had generated. Errors resemble novice errors: not tracing, tracing wrongly, wrong line numbers.
numbers: 399 questions (798 answers). GPT-3.5 69% overall, GPT-4 88% (47 vs 122 incorrect, 61% fewer). VariableTrace GPT-3.5 55%. LoopEnd GPT-3.5 40% vs GPT-4 91-100%. GPT-4 hallucinated more to justify wrong answers.
limits: Questions came from LLM code, not student code; multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Even strong models lose where loops are traced; add a held-out trace check.

source: Fan et al. (2023) Exploring the Potential of Large Language Models in Generating Code-Tracing Questions for Introductory Programming Courses
finding: From a search summary only: GPT-4 wrote code-tracing questions close to human-written ones.
numbers: Clarity 4.42 vs 4.72 (1-5 scale); about 56% of GPT-4 questions mistaken for human-written (search snippet, unverified).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Low: about question writing, not tracing accuracy.

source: Jain, Do, Wu, Wang (2026) A Plan-Tracing Interface for AI-Supported Algorithm Planning
finding: Learners simulate the algorithm in their plan on a concrete input (plan tracing), then get LLM feedback. Tracing gave fewer code-like steps and more goal-driven plans; no detectable difference in LLM feedback quality.
numbers: Exploratory between-subjects study, N=20 students, with or without the plan-tracing interface.
limits: Tiny N, exploratory. A human learner study with an AI tool, not an LLM tracing test.
agent_relevance: Tracing on a concrete input before code exists is possible, but no feedback gain was found, so keep it conditional.

source: Abdollahi et al. (2025) Demystifying Errors in LLM Reasoning Traces: An Empirical Study of Code Execution Simulation
finding: Reasoning LLMs (DeepSeek-R1, o4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude 4 Sonnet) reach high output accuracy; trace errors cluster in arithmetic and a calculator-style tool fixed over half of them.
numbers: 427 snippets (HumanEval+, LiveCodeBench) x 12 inputs (regular, edge, invalid). Accuracy 85% to 98%. Nine error categories; Computation Errors most common, then control flow. Tool-augmented reasoning corrected 58% of sampled computation errors.
limits: Tool test was run on one error category only.
agent_relevance: Hand arithmetic and indexing to code (G5). The trace may be right in structure but wrong in computation.

source: Spiess, Devanbu, Barr (2026) How Robustly do LLMs Understand Execution Semantics?
finding: Near-perfect CruxEval hides brittleness: perturbed inputs and exceptions break frontier models, and many models are inconsistent across nearby inputs for one program.
numbers: 14 models. GPT-5.2: 99% on original CruxEval, but accuracy fell 19.52 points under perturbation and PSR (all perturbed inputs right) was 56.14; GPT-5 Nano PSR 82.75; Gemini 3 Pro PSR 97.16. DeepSeek-R1 family 38% to 67% but stable.
limits: Exception prediction depended on prompt wording (the original CruxEval prompt never mentions exceptions).
agent_relevance: Agreement on one input proves little. Run mutated inputs (G3) and treat exceptions as a separate case.

source: Yan et al. (2025) STEPWISE-CODEX-Bench: Evaluating Complex Multi-Function Comprehension and Fine-Grained Execution Reasoning
finding: CRUXEval is saturated (best models over 95%); asking for the number of computation steps across chained functions and nested loops separates models again.
numbers: 20+ models (14 reasoning-enhanced). o3 reaches 78.37% on the Hard-Reasoning subset (504 items).
limits: Step count is one proxy for understanding.
agent_relevance: Step counts are a cheap code-checkable probe of whether the model really ran the loop.

source: Yang, Dai, Vasilakis, Rinard (2025) Evaluating the Generalization Capabilities of Large Language Models on Code Reasoning
finding: Older models act like pattern matchers on mutated programs; the latest reasoning models generalize. 10 models, four program sources plus mutated versions.
numbers: LLM-List: DeepSeek-Coder loses about 54 points original to mutated; Qwen coder 26-35 points; QwQ, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini lose at most 4 points (o3-mini near perfect). Reversion rate above 50% for DeepSeek-Coder, 22-30% for Qwen coder.
limits: Mostly list-manipulation programs.
agent_relevance: Mutation is the right held-out check (G3). For non-reasoning models expect pattern-match errors.

source: Ding et al. (2025) LongReasonArena: A Long Reasoning Benchmark for Large Language Models
finding: Executing multi-step algorithms in text: accuracy falls linearly with log of required steps, where steps are executed lines of the solution code.
numbers: 12 models. Level 1/2/3 need about 1K / 100K / 1M reasoning tokens. DeepSeek-R1 7.5% at Level 3. Linear decline with log(array length), R2 = 0.975.
limits: Tasks include retrieval and backtracking, not only code tracing.
agent_relevance: A long trace cannot be done reliably in text. Past about 100 steps use code-run (S2 with a tool).
